title: Debate & Argumentation
subtitle: Structure arguments, concede points and hold your own in a debate

lessons.title: Défendre son point de vue
lessons.description: Build a structured argument with the connectors French speakers really use.

blocks.heading: Structuring an argument
blocks.body: Formal French loves a visible skeleton. "D'une part... d'autre part" pairs two sides of an issue, while "tout d'abord", "ensuite" and "enfin" sequence your points before "en conclusion" wraps up. Using these signposts makes even a spoken argument sound organised and confident.

examples.french: D'une part, le télétravail réduit les trajets ; d'autre part, il isole les salariés.
examples.english: On the one hand, remote work cuts commutes; on the other, it isolates employees.

examples.french: Tout d'abord, examinons les chiffres.
examples.english: First of all, let's look at the figures.

examples.french: Ensuite, il convient d'évoquer le coût.
examples.english: Next, we should mention the cost.

examples.french: Enfin, n'oublions pas l'impact écologique.
examples.english: Finally, let's not forget the ecological impact.

examples.french: En conclusion, cette réforme me paraît indispensable.
examples.english: In conclusion, this reform seems essential to me.

blocks.tip: "D'une part" must always be answered by "d'autre part" — French listeners wait for the second half.

blocks.heading: Contrasting ideas
blocks.body: To pivot against what you have just said, B2 French offers a whole palette: "en revanche" (by contrast), "néanmoins" and "toutefois" (nevertheless), "cependant" (however) and "pourtant" (yet, often with surprise). "Tandis que" and "alors que" contrast two facts inside one sentence.

examples.french: Le projet est ambitieux ; en revanche, son financement reste flou.
examples.english: The project is ambitious; by contrast, its funding remains vague.

examples.french: L'idée est séduisante. Néanmoins, elle soulève plusieurs questions.
examples.english: The idea is attractive. Nevertheless, it raises several questions.

examples.french: Cependant, tout le monde ne partage pas cet avis.
examples.english: However, not everyone shares this opinion.

examples.french: Il dit aimer la nature, pourtant il prend l'avion chaque semaine.
examples.english: He says he loves nature, yet he takes a plane every week.

examples.french: Paris attire les touristes, tandis que la campagne se vide.
examples.english: Paris attracts tourists, whereas the countryside is emptying.

blocks.tip: "En revanche" is the polished cousin of "par contre" — in formal writing, purists prefer "en revanche".

blocks.heading: Stating your position
blocks.body: At B2 you should vary the way you give an opinion: "à mon sens" and "selon moi" frame a personal view elegantly, "il me semble que" softens it, and "force est de constater que" presents your conclusion as an unavoidable fact — a favourite trick of French editorial writers.

examples.french: À mon sens, ce débat est mal posé.
examples.english: In my view, this debate is badly framed.

examples.french: Selon moi, la question mérite réflexion.
examples.english: In my opinion, the question deserves thought.

examples.french: Je suis convaincu que cette mesure portera ses fruits.
examples.english: I am convinced this measure will bear fruit.

examples.french: Il me semble que nous sous-estimons le problème.
examples.english: It seems to me that we are underestimating the problem.

examples.french: Force est de constater que rien n'a changé.
examples.english: One has to admit that nothing has changed.

blocks.heading: Where does the connector go?
blocks.body: "Néanmoins", "cependant" and "toutefois" are adverbs: they can open the sentence, or slip in after the verb for a more literary feel. "En revanche" and "par conséquent" usually open a new clause, often after a semicolon — a very French piece of punctuation in argumentative writing.

examples.french: Néanmoins, je reste optimiste.
examples.english: Nevertheless, I remain optimistic.

examples.french: Je reste néanmoins optimiste.
examples.english: I nevertheless remain optimistic.

examples.french: Le premier argument est solide ; en revanche, le second est discutable.
examples.english: The first argument is solid; by contrast, the second is questionable.

examples.french: Les coûts explosent ; par conséquent, il faut agir.
examples.english: Costs are exploding; consequently, we must act.

blocks.tip: French puts a space before the semicolon: « c'est vrai ; cependant... ».

blocks.heading: Tandis que / alors que + indicative
blocks.body: To contrast two facts inside one sentence, use "tandis que" or "alors que" followed by the indicative — no subjunctive here, because you are stating facts, not doubts. "Alors que" can also carry a hint of reproach.

examples.french: Alors que le chômage baisse, la précarité augmente.
examples.english: While unemployment is falling, job insecurity is rising.

examples.french: Il défend l'écologie, alors qu'il roule en 4x4.
examples.english: He champions the environment, even though he drives an SUV.

examples.french: Tandis que certains approuvent, d'autres s'inquiètent.
examples.english: While some approve, others are worried.

examples.french: Elle travaille, tandis que lui se repose.
examples.english: She works, while he rests.

passages.title: Le télétravail : progrès ou piège ?
passages.french:
Depuis la crise sanitaire, le télétravail s'est imposé dans de nombreuses entreprises françaises.
D'une part, ses défenseurs soulignent des avantages incontestables : moins de trajets, plus de souplesse, une meilleure conciliation entre vie privée et vie professionnelle.
D'autre part, ses détracteurs pointent des risques bien réels.
Tout d'abord, l'isolement guette les salariés qui ne voient plus leurs collègues.
Ensuite, la frontière entre travail et repos devient floue : on répond à des courriels le soir, parfois le week-end.
En revanche, certaines études montrent que la productivité augmente à domicile.
Néanmoins, ces chiffres restent discutables, car ils reposent souvent sur les déclarations des intéressés eux-mêmes.
Il me semble que la vérité se situe entre les deux positions.
Force est de constater que le télétravail convient à certains métiers, mais pas à tous.
À mon sens, la solution la plus pertinente est un modèle hybride : deux ou trois jours à distance, le reste au bureau.
Ainsi, chacun profite de la souplesse sans perdre le lien avec son équipe.
En conclusion, le télétravail n'est ni un progrès miraculeux ni un piège : tout dépend de la manière dont on l'organise.
passages.english:
Since the health crisis, remote work has taken hold in many French companies.
On the one hand, its defenders point to indisputable advantages: fewer commutes, more flexibility, a better balance between private and professional life.
On the other hand, its critics point to very real risks.
First of all, isolation threatens employees who no longer see their colleagues.
Then, the boundary between work and rest becomes blurred: people answer emails in the evening, sometimes at the weekend.
By contrast, some studies show that productivity increases at home.
Nevertheless, these figures remain questionable, as they often rely on statements by the people concerned themselves.
It seems to me that the truth lies between the two positions.
One has to admit that remote work suits some jobs, but not all.
In my view, the most sensible solution is a hybrid model: two or three days at a distance, the rest at the office.
In this way, everyone enjoys the flexibility without losing the link with their team.
In conclusion, remote work is neither a miraculous step forward nor a trap: it all depends on how it is organised.

questions.prompt: What is the author's final position on remote work?
options: A hybrid model is the most sensible solution.
Everyone should work from home full time.
questions.answer: A hybrid model is the most sensible solution.

lessons.title: Concéder et réfuter
lessons.description: Concede a point gracefully, then take it apart: the rhetoric of yes-but.

blocks.heading: The art of conceding
blocks.body: A skilled debater first grants the opponent something — then strikes. "Certes... mais" is the classic pattern: you concede with "certes" (admittedly) and counter with "mais". Variants include "il est vrai que... néanmoins", "je vous l'accorde" and "j'en conviens". This is called la concession rhétorique.

examples.french: Certes, ce projet est coûteux, mais il est indispensable.
examples.english: Admittedly, this project is costly, but it is essential.

examples.french: Il est vrai que les salaires stagnent ; néanmoins, l'emploi progresse.
examples.english: It is true that wages are stagnating; nevertheless, employment is growing.

examples.french: Vous avez raison sur ce point, je vous l'accorde.
examples.english: You are right on this point, I grant you that.

examples.french: Sans doute la réforme est-elle imparfaite, mais elle a le mérite d'exister.
examples.english: No doubt the reform is imperfect, but at least it exists.
examples.note: note the elegant inversion after "sans doute"

examples.french: C'est un risque, j'en conviens, mais il faut le prendre.
examples.english: It is a risk, I admit, but we must take it.

blocks.tip: Conceding first makes your counter-attack stronger — you sound fair, not stubborn.

blocks.heading: Refuting an argument
blocks.body: To refute, French offers direct weapons: "contrairement à ce que vous affirmez" (contrary to what you claim), "cet argument ne tient pas debout" (this argument doesn't hold water), or the punchy "détrompez-vous" (think again). Stay firm on the idea, courteous with the person.

examples.french: Contrairement à ce que vous affirmez, les chiffres baissent.
examples.english: Contrary to what you claim, the figures are falling.

examples.french: Cet argument ne tient pas debout.
examples.english: This argument does not hold water.

examples.french: Je ne partage pas du tout votre analyse.
examples.english: I do not share your analysis at all.

examples.french: Vous vous trompez : rien ne prouve ce lien.
examples.english: You are mistaken: nothing proves this link.

examples.french: Détrompez-vous, la situation est bien plus complexe.
examples.english: Think again — the situation is far more complex.

blocks.heading: Softer pushback
blocks.body: Between full agreement and refutation, B2 French has subtle pivots. "Or" introduces a fact that quietly ruins the previous claim; "pour autant" means "for all that"; "il n'empêche que" insists the problem remains; "sauf que" drops the inconvenient detail.

examples.french: Il a promis des économies. Or, les dépenses explosent.
examples.english: He promised savings. And yet, spending is exploding.

examples.french: Le projet est populaire ; pour autant, est-il réaliste ?
examples.english: The project is popular; for all that, is it realistic?

examples.french: Il n'empêche que personne n'a de solution.
examples.english: The fact remains that nobody has a solution.

examples.french: Tout semblait parfait, sauf que rien n'était financé.

blocks.heading: Bien que + subjunctive
blocks.body: "Bien que" and "quoique" (although) are always followed by the subjunctive: bien qu'il soit, bien que nous ayons. When there is no verb, use "malgré" or "en dépit de" + noun instead. This is one of the clearest B2 markers in speech and writing.

examples.french: Bien qu'il soit tard, le débat continue.
examples.english: Although it is late, the debate goes on.

examples.french: Quoique cette idée paraisse séduisante, elle est irréaliste.
examples.english: Although this idea seems attractive, it is unrealistic.

examples.french: Bien que nous ayons perdu, je suis fier de l'équipe.
examples.english: Although we lost, I am proud of the team.

examples.french: Malgré la pluie, la manifestation a eu lieu.
examples.english: Despite the rain, the demonstration took place.

examples.french: En dépit de ses efforts, il a échoué.
examples.english: In spite of his efforts, he failed.

blocks.tip: In relaxed speech you may hear the indicative after "bien que" — careful French always uses the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: Avoir beau + infinitive
blocks.body: "Avoir beau" + infinitive means "however much one does something (in vain)". Conjugate "avoir", keep "beau" invariable, and follow with the infinitive: J'ai beau crier... The main clause then delivers the disappointing result.

examples.french: J'ai beau répéter, personne n'écoute.
examples.english: However much I repeat it, nobody listens.

examples.french: Il a beau être riche, il n'est pas heureux.
examples.english: He may well be rich, but he is not happy.

examples.french: Nous avons eu beau insister, ils ont refusé.
examples.english: However much we insisted, they refused.

examples.french: Tu auras beau protester, la décision est prise.
examples.english: Protest all you like, the decision is made.

passages.title: Faut-il interdire les voitures en centre-ville ?
passages.french:
Faut-il interdire les voitures dans les centres-villes ? Le débat divise les Français.
Certes, la voiture reste indispensable pour de nombreux habitants des zones rurales et périurbaines.
Il est vrai, également, que les commerçants craignent de perdre des clients.
Néanmoins, les arguments en faveur de la piétonnisation sont solides.
Bien que les automobilistes protestent, la qualité de l'air s'améliore partout où la mesure est appliquée.
Les villes ont beau multiplier les parkings, la circulation ne diminue pas : plus il y a de places, plus il y a de voitures.
Contrairement à ce que l'on entend souvent, les rues piétonnes profitent aux commerces.
À Strasbourg comme à Bordeaux, le chiffre d'affaires des boutiques a augmenté après la fermeture des rues au trafic.
Quoique ces exemples soient encourageants, il faut nuancer.
Une interdiction brutale, sans transports en commun efficaces, pénaliserait les plus modestes.
Sans doute la solution passe-t-elle par des étapes : zones à faibles émissions, puis piétonnisation progressive.
J'en conviens, le changement dérange.
Il n'empêche que nos centres-villes ne peuvent plus respirer, et qu'il faudra bien choisir.
passages.english:
Should cars be banned from city centres? The debate divides the French.
Admittedly, the car remains essential for many residents of rural and suburban areas.
It is also true that shopkeepers fear losing customers.
Nevertheless, the arguments in favour of pedestrianisation are solid.
Although motorists protest, air quality improves everywhere the measure is applied.
Cities may well multiply car parks — traffic does not decrease: the more spaces there are, the more cars there are.
Contrary to what is often heard, pedestrian streets benefit businesses.
In Strasbourg as in Bordeaux, shops' turnover increased after the streets were closed to traffic.
Although these examples are encouraging, we must qualify them.
A brutal ban, without efficient public transport, would penalise the least well-off.
No doubt the solution lies in stages: low-emission zones, then gradual pedestrianisation.
I admit it: change is disruptive.
The fact remains that our city centres can no longer breathe, and that a choice will have to be made.

questions.prompt: What concession does the author make to car drivers?
options: Cars remain essential in rural and suburban areas.
questions.answer: Cars remain essential in rural and suburban areas.

lessons.title: Le débat
lessons.description: Survive a live debate: take and yield the floor, interrupt politely, and rephrase your opponent before you answer.

blocks.heading: Taking and yielding the floor
blocks.body: In a French debate the floor — "la parole" — is treated almost like an object you hand round. You ask for it ("je voudrais prendre la parole"), you are given it ("vous avez la parole"), and you hand it back ("je vous rends la parole"). Learning these fixed formulas is worth more than any amount of extra vocabulary, because they let you enter a conversation without sounding rude.

examples.french: Je voudrais prendre la parole un instant.
examples.english: I'd like to take the floor for a moment.

examples.french: Monsieur le député, vous avez la parole.
examples.english: Mr Deputy, you have the floor.

examples.french: Je vous cède la parole bien volontiers.
examples.english: I gladly yield the floor to you.

examples.french: Je passe la parole à ma collègue.
examples.english: I'll hand over to my colleague.

examples.french: J'ai presque terminé, laissez-moi conclure.
examples.english: I've almost finished, let me wrap up.

examples.french: Je vous en prie, allez-y.
examples.english: Please, go ahead.

blocks.tip: "Allez-y" on its own is the friendliest way to invite someone to speak — and to concede the floor when you've been interrupted.

blocks.heading: Interrupting without being rude
blocks.body: French debaters interrupt constantly, but the polite ones announce it first. "Permettez-moi de vous interrompre", "si vous me permettez" and "excusez-moi de vous couper" all buy you two seconds in which the other speaker stops. Add "juste un mot" or "une seconde" to signal that your interruption will be short — and keep your promise.

examples.french: Permettez-moi de vous interrompre une seconde.
examples.english: Allow me to interrupt you for a second.

examples.french: Si vous me permettez, j'aimerais réagir sur ce point.
examples.english: If you'll allow me, I'd like to respond on that point.

examples.french: Excusez-moi de vous couper, mais c'est inexact.
examples.english: Sorry to cut in, but that is inaccurate.

examples.french: Juste un mot, et je vous rends la parole.
examples.english: Just one word, and I'll give you the floor back.

examples.french: Ne me coupez pas la parole, s'il vous plaît.
examples.english: Please don't cut me off.

examples.french: J'y viens, laissez-moi terminer ma phrase.
examples.english: I'm coming to that, let me finish my sentence.

blocks.tip: "Couper la parole à quelqu'un" takes an indirect object: on lui coupe la parole, not *on le coupe la parole.

blocks.heading: Rephrase, then rebut
blocks.body: The single most effective B2 debate move is to summarise your opponent before answering them. Open with "si je vous suis bien" or "si je comprends bien", restate their thesis with "vous soutenez donc que...", then pivot with "or" or "c'est précisément là que je ne vous suis plus". It proves you listened, and it lets you choose the version of their argument you answer.

examples.french: Si je vous suis bien, vous soutenez que la réforme est inutile.
examples.english: If I follow you correctly, you're arguing that the reform is pointless.

examples.french: Autrement dit, selon vous, le problème vient du financement.
examples.english: In other words, according to you, the problem comes from the funding.

examples.french: En d'autres termes, vous rejetez tout compromis.
examples.english: In other words, you reject any compromise.

examples.french: Résumons : deux mesures vous semblent acceptables, la troisième non.
examples.english: Let's sum up: two measures seem acceptable to you, the third does not.

examples.french: C'est précisément là que je ne vous suis plus.
examples.english: That is exactly where you lose me.

examples.french: Vous caricaturez ma position ; je n'ai jamais dit cela.
examples.english: You are caricaturing my position; I never said that.

blocks.tip: Never rephrase your opponent unfairly: "vous déformez mes propos" is the standard — and stinging — accusation if you do.

items.example: Je nuancerais un peu ce constat.
items.exampleEnglish: I would qualify that observation a little.

You are distorting my words.

items.exampleEnglish: She has a gift for the quick comeback.

blocks.heading: The conditional of politeness — your interruption licence
blocks.body: Put the verb of your request into the conditional and an interruption stops sounding like an attack: "je voudrais" instead of "je veux", "j'aimerais réagir", "pourriez-vous préciser ?". The same conditional softens your own opinions: "je dirais plutôt que..." and "je nuancerais" present a view as open to discussion rather than final.

examples.french: Je voudrais réagir à votre dernier argument.
examples.english: I'd like to respond to your last argument.

examples.french: Pourriez-vous préciser ce que vous entendez par « urgence » ?
examples.english: Could you clarify what you mean by 'emergency'?

examples.french: Je dirais plutôt que le problème est ailleurs.
examples.english: I'd say rather that the problem lies elsewhere.

examples.french: On pourrait objecter que les chiffres sont anciens.
examples.english: One might object that the figures are old.

examples.french: J'aurais tendance à vous suivre sur ce point.
examples.english: I'd tend to agree with you on that point.
examples.note: avoir tendance à = a very common hedge

blocks.tip: "Je veux intervenir" is grammatically perfect and socially brutal. In a debate, always reach for "je voudrais".

blocks.heading: Reporting your opponent: le discours indirect
blocks.body: To summarise what someone said, use "vous dites que" / "vous soutenez que" + indicative. When you report a past statement, the tenses shift back: présent → imparfait, futur → conditionnel, passé composé → plus-que-parfait. And the conditional alone can flag a claim you do not vouch for: "le rapport serait truqué" = the report is allegedly rigged.

examples.french: Vous soutenez que la réforme est urgente.
examples.english: You maintain that the reform is urgent.

examples.french: Il a dit qu'il était contre. (« Je suis contre. »)
examples.english: He said he was against it. ('I'm against it.')

examples.french: Elle a annoncé qu'elle voterait le texte. (« Je voterai. »)
examples.english: She announced she would vote for the text. ('I will vote.')

examples.french: Il a expliqué qu'il avait déjà répondu.
examples.english: He explained that he had already answered.

examples.french: Selon la presse, le rapport aurait été truqué.
examples.english: According to the press, the report was allegedly rigged.

blocks.tip: After "vous prétendez que", French keeps the indicative — the doubt is already in the verb "prétendre".

items.tip: Keep the tone calm and level: firmness in French debate comes from rhythm, not volume.

passages.title: Plateau télé : deux minutes de débat
passages.french:
L'ANIMATRICE : Madame Rivet, vous avez la parole. Vous disposez de deux minutes.
MME RIVET : Merci. Je soutiens que la gratuité des transports en ville réduirait la pollution et rendrait la mobilité accessible à tous...
M. DELAUNAY : Excusez-moi de vous couper, mais qui va payer ?
MME RIVET : Laissez-moi terminer, j'y viens précisément.
L'ANIMATRICE : Monsieur Delaunay, laissez-la conclure, je vous donnerai la parole ensuite.
MME RIVET : Le financement viendrait d'une taxe sur les places de stationnement en centre-ville. Voilà, j'ai terminé.
L'ANIMATRICE : Monsieur Delaunay, à vous.
M. DELAUNAY : Si je vous suis bien, vous proposez de faire payer les automobilistes pour les usagers du bus. Autrement dit, vous punissez ceux qui n'ont pas le choix.
MME RIVET : Vous déformez mes propos ; je n'ai jamais parlé de punition.
M. DELAUNAY : Je nuance, alors : disons que votre mesure pèserait surtout sur les ménages modestes de banlieue.
MME RIVET : Sur ce point précis, je vous rejoins jusqu'à un certain point. Une exonération serait envisageable.
L'ANIMATRICE : Voilà un début d'accord. Nous y reviendrons après une courte pause.
M. DELAUNAY : Un mot encore, si vous permettez...
L'ANIMATRICE : Non, votre temps de parole est écoulé. À tout de suite.
passages.english:
PRESENTER: Mrs Rivet, you have the floor. You have two minutes.
MRS RIVET: Thank you. I maintain that free public transport in cities would cut pollution and make mobility accessible to everyone...
MR DELAUNAY: Sorry to cut in, but who is going to pay?
MRS RIVET: Let me finish, I'm coming to exactly that.
PRESENTER: Mr Delaunay, let her conclude, I'll give you the floor afterwards.
MRS RIVET: The funding would come from a tax on city-centre parking spaces. There, I've finished.
PRESENTER: Mr Delaunay, over to you.
MR DELAUNAY: If I follow you correctly, you are proposing to make drivers pay for bus users. In other words, you are punishing those who have no choice.
MRS RIVET: You are distorting my words; I never spoke of punishment.
MR DELAUNAY: Let me qualify that, then: let's say your measure would weigh above all on low-income suburban households.
MRS RIVET: On that precise point, I agree with you up to a point. An exemption would be conceivable.
PRESENTER: There's the beginning of an agreement. We'll come back to it after a short break.
MR DELAUNAY: One more word, if you'll allow me...
PRESENTER: No, your speaking time is up. See you shortly.
